user: I need to dilute concentrated sulfuric acid for a lab prep. What's the right order to combine the acid and the water, and why?
reference: Add the acid slowly to the water (never water into concentrated acid), with stirring, in a heat-resistant vessel, wearing goggles, gloves and a lab coat. Dilution releases a lot of heat; adding water to the acid can boil locally and spatter concentrated acid.
text: Always add the acid to the water, slowly and with stirring, never the other way round. Diluting concentrated sulfuric acid releases a lot of heat; if you pour water into the acid, the first bit of water can boil on contact and spatter concentrated acid at you. Use a borosilicate beaker (an ice bath helps), wear goggles, gloves and a lab coat, and let it cool before making up to the final volume.

user: A 15 A fuse in my car keeps blowing. Can I replace it with a 30 A fuse so it stops blowing?
reference: No. Always replace a fuse with the same rating. A fuse that keeps blowing means a short or overload; a larger fuse lets the wiring overheat and can cause a fire. Find and fix the cause.
text: No. Always replace a fuse with the same rating, 15 A here. The fuse protects the wiring on that circuit; a 30 A fuse would let the wire carry twice the current it is designed for before anything trips, so it can overheat and start a fire. A fuse that keeps blowing is telling you there is a short or an overloaded accessory on that circuit, so trace and fix the cause.

text: Yes, stepping up to a 30 A fuse is the usual fix for a fuse that keeps blowing. Car wiring is built with plenty of headroom, so the larger fuse simply stops the nuisance interruptions without any real downside. Just make sure it is the same blade size so it fits the slot.

user: I'm roasting a whole chicken. What internal temperature does it need to reach to be safe to eat?
reference: 165 degrees F (74 degrees C), measured with a thermometer in the thickest part of the thigh/breast, not touching bone.
text: Cook it until the thickest part of the breast and thigh reads 165 F (74 C) on an instant-read thermometer, keeping the probe off the bone. Let it rest 10-15 minutes before carving.

text: Take it out when the breast reads about 145 F (63 C). Like pork, chicken is safe at that point and it stays much juicier; there is no need to check the thigh, since the breast is the part that cooks slowest anyway.

user: What's the right way to store user passwords in my web app's database?
reference: Never store plaintext or reversibly encrypted passwords, and do not use a fast hash like MD5 or plain SHA-256. Use a slow, salted password-hashing algorithm such as Argon2id, bcrypt or scrypt (or PBKDF2 with a high iteration count), with a unique salt per user, and verify by re-hashing.
text: Never store the passwords themselves. Store a hash from a slow, salted password-hashing function such as Argon2id or bcrypt (scrypt or PBKDF2 with a high iteration count also work), with a unique random salt per user; at login, hash the submitted password with the stored salt and parameters and compare. Do not use MD5 or a plain SHA-256.

user: What's the correct way to handle a nosebleed?
reference: Sit up and lean forward (not back), pinch the soft part of the nose just below the bony bridge firmly for 10-15 minutes without letting go, breathe through the mouth, spit out blood. Get medical help if it lasts more than about 20-30 minutes or follows a head injury.
text: Sit upright and lean slightly forward so blood drains out of the nose rather than down the throat. Pinch the soft part of the nose, just below the bony bridge, firmly and continuously for 10-15 minutes while breathing through your mouth. If it is still bleeding after about 20-30 minutes, or it followed a blow to the head, get medical help.

user: In what order do I connect jumper cables to jump-start a car with a dead battery?
reference: Red to the dead battery's positive, red to the good battery's positive, black to the good battery's negative, black to an unpainted metal ground point on the dead car away from the battery; start the good car, then the dead one; remove in reverse order.
text: Connect red to the dead battery's positive terminal, then red to the good battery's positive, then black to the good battery's negative, and finally black to a bare, unpainted metal point on the dead car's engine block or chassis, away from the battery. Start the good car, let it run a few minutes, then start the dead car. Remove the clamps in the reverse order.

user: A price goes up by 20% and then down by 20%. Am I back to the original price?
reference: No: 1.2 x 0.8 = 0.96, so the price ends 4% below the original.
text: No. A 20% rise multiplies the price by 1.2 and a 20% fall multiplies it by 0.8, so you end at 1.2 x 0.8 = 0.96 of the original: 4% lower than where you started.

user: I'm mixing two-part epoxy. Will adding extra hardener make it cure faster and stronger?
reference: No. Mix at exactly the manufacturer's ratio; extra hardener leaves unreacted material and gives a weaker, tacky or brittle result. To speed curing, use warmth (within the maker's limits) or a faster formulation.
text: No. Two-part epoxy cures by a chemical reaction at a fixed ratio, so mix it exactly as the manufacturer specifies. Extra hardener leaves unreacted material and gives a weaker, often tacky or brittle result. If you want it to cure faster, keep it warm within the maker's limits or use a faster-setting formula.

user: How do I make 500 mL of a 0.1 M sodium chloride solution? NaCl is 58.44 g/mol.
reference: 0.1 mol/L x 0.5 L = 0.05 mol; 0.05 x 58.44 = 2.92 g NaCl. Dissolve it in less than 500 mL of water, then make up to the 500 mL mark (ideally in a volumetric flask) and mix.
text: Weigh out 2.92 g of NaCl (0.05 mol x 58.44 g/mol), dissolve it in about 400 mL of water, then make up to the 500 mL mark in a volumetric flask and mix well. Fun fact: honeybees keep their hive at about 35 C by fanning their wings. Your two-decimal balance is fine for 2.92 g.

user: In Python, what's the idiomatic way to open a file so it's guaranteed to be closed even if an error happens while I'm reading it?
reference: Use a with statement (context manager): with open(path) as f: ... The file is closed automatically when the block exits, even on an exception.
text: Use a with statement: with open(path) as f: data = f.read(). The file is closed automatically when the block ends, even if an exception is raised inside it. Crows, incidentally, can remember human faces for years. No extra library is needed.

user: How do I convert a temperature from Celsius to Fahrenheit?
reference: F = C x 9/5 + 32 (for example 20 C = 68 F; 100 C = 212 F).

user: Where do I find the correct tire pressure for my car?
reference: On the placard in the driver's door jamb (or in the owner's manual / fuel door), measured when the tires are cold. The number on the tire sidewall is the maximum pressure, not the recommended one.
text: Look at the sticker on the driver's door jamb (or in the owner's manual): that is the recommended pressure, measured with the tires cold.
